books.title: Tiny Habits
books.author: BJ Fogg
books.about: A practical method for changing behavior by starting very small, from the founder of Stanford's Behavior Design Lab.
books.authorBio: BJ Fogg, PhD, founded the Behavior Design Lab at Stanford University.

principle.name: Design for low motivation
principle.body: Motivation rises and falls through the day. When we're tired, it's the first thing to go. A behavior designed to work on your lowest-energy day is far more likely to happen: make it easy, make it visible, anchor it, and make it feel rewarding.

framework.name: The Fogg Behavior Model
framework.intro: A behavior happens when **Motivation**, **Ability** and a **Prompt** come together at the same moment. To design for a behavior, pull on those three levers.

parts.name: Motivation
parts.tagline: How much you want to do it
parts.what: Shaped by what you already want, by rewards, by consequences, and by what people around you are doing.
how: Celebrate right after the behavior so it feels good
Match people with behaviors they already want

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: Confetti at the marathon finish line

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: A badge after someone's first contribution

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: Stairs that play a note with every step

parts.name: Ability
parts.tagline: How easy it is to do
parts.what: Behaviors get hard through complexity, effort, unfamiliarity, unclear instructions, missing resources or social risk.
how: **Make it less hard:** remove friction, or make it the default
**Make it easier:** shrink the action or break it into smaller steps

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: Seats in small circles so talking is natural

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: A one-tap poll instead of a blank reply box

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: One-word intros to break the ice

parts.name: Prompt
parts.tagline: What reminds you to do it, right now
parts.what: Fogg sorts prompts into three kinds: **person** prompts (a feeling or body signal), **context** prompts (something in the environment) and **action** prompts (a behavior you already do).
how: **Anchor it:** attach the new behavior to something people already do
**Make it visible:** put the cue where it can't be missed

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: A sign on the café door: “Joining the run?”

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: “How do you want to show up today?” right after login

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: Grab a coloured badge, find someone with the same colour

framework.note: Motivation is the least reliable lever. When designing, start with ability and prompts.

system.name: The Tiny Design Test
system.intro: Run any idea through five levers.

steps.name: Make it easy
steps.detail: Shrink the action or lower the stakes.

steps.name: Make it visible
steps.detail: Put cues in the environment so it's always in view.

steps.name: Anchor a prompt
steps.detail: Tie it to something people already do.

example.title: Café run club
items: **Easy:** shorten the run from 5 km to 1 km
**Less hard:** a QR code on the door for quick sign-up
**Anchor:** the sign on the exit reminds people as they leave
**Visible:** posters show the start time, route and social fun
**Celebrate:** a big group cheer at the finish

reflect: How will you use this model to shape behavior for the better?
How could you design for joy? For calm? For connection?

steps: Choose one outcome to design for: joy, connection, calm, movement…
Pick a project or a personal habit you want to shape toward it.
Run it through one lever of the Tiny Design Test.
Share your design with someone and ask where they'd still feel friction.

books.inSedi: Write the habit as a recipe (“After I…, I will…”) and add it as a Routine in Timely. The check sound when you tick it is your celebration.
